title: Soldiers in the Capital: Why the National Guard Is Staying in D.C. Until 2029
summary: Have you ever seen soldiers patrolling your neighborhood? In Washington, D.C., kids have been seeing them for a whole year — and they’re not leaving anytime soon. President Trump sent the National Guard to the city in August 2025, saying there was a crime emergency. Now, the mission has been extended all the way to January 2029. That’s three more years! More than 4,600 troops from 24 states and territories are still there. You might spot them near the Tidal Basin during the Cherry Blossom Festival or in Georgetown, where serious crimes are rare. They’ve helped with things like snow removal and even medical emergencies. Some people like that. But others feel like they’re living in a “police state” — where the government uses too much force. The ACLU, a group that protects people’s rights, says there’s no real emergency anymore. Crime was already going down before the troops arrived. In fact, overall crime dropped 20% this year, and homicides fell by 32% — from 97 to 66. But experts aren’t sure if the soldiers caused that drop. Keeping the Guard in D.C. until 2029 will cost about $1.4 billion. That’s enough to buy every kid in the city a new bicycle — twice! City leaders like council member Brianne K. Nadeau say it’s “demoralizing” to see soldiers every day with no end in sight. Because D.C. isn’t a state, the president has more control here than in other places. A lawsuit is trying to stop the deployment, but many people aren’t hopeful. In the recent elections, voters chose candidates who want more freedom for D.C. One of them, Janeese Lewis George, could become the next mayor. Trump has already warned he might take over the city if she wins. For now, the soldiers stay — and kids in the capital keep seeing them on their streets.
why_it_matters: It shows how the government can send soldiers into a city, which changes how safe and free kids feel when they walk to school or the park.

background_read: The National Guard is a reserve military force — unlike regular soldiers, they normally live at home and train part-time, but a president or governor can call them up for duty.
Washington, D.C., the capital of the United States, is not a state, so the federal government (including the president) has more power over it than over other places in the country.
In American history, troops have sometimes been sent into cities during big protests or after disasters, but keeping them in a city for years during peacetime is very unusual.
